messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prison Guard
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 42

**Patient Vignette: Marcus R.**

Marcus is a 28-year-old married Latin American man who works as a prison guard at a maximum-security facility. He presents for his third session today, sitting forward in his chair, his large frame tense and coiled. He has not made eye contact since he sat down.

His story begins eighteen months ago, on a night that started like any other. Marcus was working the 4-to-midnight shift in C-block. His best friend and training partner, Diego, was on the same floor. They had been through the academy together, had each other’s backs during riots, and spent weekends fixing up Diego’s old Chevrolet. Marcus remembers the sound of the alarm—not the regular cell-door buzzer, but the piercing, sustained tone that means a life is in danger. He ran toward the noise. An inmate had attacked Diego from behind with a shank made from a melted toothbrush. Marcus was the first one there. He held Diego’s head in his hands, trying to stop the bleeding, shouting for help. Diego looked at him, tried to say something, and then went still. Marcus performed CPR until the medics arrived, but he knew. He knew before they did. Diego was gone.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus didn’t cry. He went back to work after three days. He told his wife, Elena, that he had to get back on the horse, that the prison needed him, that Diego would have wanted him to keep going. But inside, something had shattered. He began to see Diego’s face everywhere. Not a ghost, but a flash—the exact moment the light left his eyes. It happens when he’s driving, when he’s trying to fall asleep, when he’s eating dinner. He will freeze mid-bite, his fork suspended in the air, seeing the blood on his own hands.

At work, he has become a different man. He used to be known as the calm one, the guard who could talk down a tense situation. Now, he is hypervigilant. He cannot stand to have an inmate behind him. He conducts pat-downs with his back to a wall, his heart hammering so hard he can hear it in his ears. He has started carrying a second, hidden knife in his boot, something he never did before. His supervisors have noticed. He was written up last month for screaming at an inmate who tapped him on the shoulder from behind.

Sleep is a battleground. He avoids it. He stays up watching old action movies until 3 a.m., knowing that when he closes his eyes, the dream will come. It is always the same: he is back in C-block, but this time, it is his wife, Elena, bleeding out on the concrete. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his hands clawing at the sheets, checking her side of the bed to make sure she is real. He has not told her about the dreams.

Elena has started to pull away. She tells him he is not present, that he is a stranger in their house. Their two-year-old daughter, Sofia, reaches for him, and he flinches. He is terrified of holding her, of the responsibility, of the fragility of her small body. He feels a constant, low-grade numbness, as if he is watching his own life from behind a thick pane of glass. He cannot feel joy. He cannot feel anger, really—just a flat, buzzing tension.

He came to therapy because Elena gave him an ultimatum. He scored a 42 on the PCL-5, a number that confirms what his body already knows: he is not okay. He is still holding Diego. He just doesn’t know how to put him down.
